Subject: Post-call recap + concurrency & rate limits follow-up

Hi Mike — thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and a few clarifying questions so we can size a proposal that matches EdgeScale's production needs.

Recap (from our discussion)
- Primary workload: real-time agent responses in the control plane + background batch embedding jobs for search.
- Peak QPS target (user-facing): ~500 qps sustained during peak windows; burst to ~1.2k qps for 1-2 minute spikes.
- Concurrency: roughly 1,000 parallel open request slots expected across regions; ~1,200 concurrent streaming sessions for live sessions.
- Latency SLO: 95th percentile token latency target ~150–200ms for generation in the primary region.
- Streaming: websocket-style streams for agent updates; we discussed using chunked HTTP/2 streaming and optional keep-alive.

Questions / items for Redwood to confirm
1) Do you expect a hard per-connection limit from the client side (e.g., X concurrent HTTP/2 streams per user)?
2) What percentage of calls will be streaming vs. non-streaming? (helps for KV cache estimates)
3) Any regulatory constraints requiring data residency (we noted US primary)?

Next steps from our side: Rafael will detail rate-limit options and a draft rate card that includes hosted vs. dedicated pricing for the concurrency profile. Marcus will write up recommended connection-pooling settings and streaming guidance. I'll assemble a short MAP and timeline and send back an initial proposal + attachments.

Attaching: redwood-ratecard-v2.pdf (draft), edgescale-map-draft.xlsx (working MAP).

Thanks — Naomi

Naomi / team — thanks for the quick recap and for capturing the MAP. A few clarifications from my side:

- We don't have a strict per-user stream cap today; the client will open multiple streams per user (2–3) during active sessions. Total active users at peak are estimated ~400–600, which yields the concurrent streaming figure I gave.
- Rough split is 70% streaming (live agent updates), 30% short non-streamed generation calls (batch-like).
- Data residency: must stay in US (primary), but we'll occasionally route EU workloads for EU customers — likely a separate contract.

On rate caps: we can be flexible on initial caps during PoC but need clear fallbacks for throttling (429 behavior and retry-after guidance). For cost planning we need a realistic hosted vs dedicated delta.

I'll review the ratecard and MAP and circle back by Tuesday. Also looped procurement for a timeline on their end.

Subject: Redwood options for rate limits, concurrency, and quotas

Hi Mike — quick note on how Redwood typically maps rate-limits to the kinds of numbers you shared, plus negotiation levers. High-level options:

1) Hosted API (fastest onboarding)   - Default control: per-API-key token-rate and per-minute token caps, plus a parallel-request cap (concurrent inference workers) at the account level.   - Typical soft defaults: 400 concurrent requests for medium accounts; we can raise to 1k+ with agreed SLAs/commits.   - Throttling behavior: 429 responses with Retry-After; we support leaky-bucket smoothing at the edge to reduce spike drops.

2) Dedicated capacity (reserved GPU pools)   - You get a pool sized to your qps + concurrency with predictable headroom, plus the option to reserve streaming-optimized instances.   - Connection limits still apply per front-end instance, but scaling is in your control (autoscale rules + burst override).

Key negotiation levers we can use for EdgeScale:
- Move from account-level concurrent cap to per-VPC/fleet caps so you won't run into noisy-neighbor issues.
- Pre-warm additional concurrency tokens for launch windows (temporary bump for first 90 days).
- Rate shaping: we can expose an edge-side smoothing policy to convert short spikes into sustained higher throughput while keeping backend stable.

Concrete ask for sizing: if you expect 1.2k bursts and sustained 500 qps, recommend provisioning for 1,200 concurrent streams and baseline 600 concurrent non-stream requests (for safety). That maps to roughly N dedicated GPU slots depending on model/sequence length — I flagged this for Marcus to convert into a rough cost estimate.

I'll attach a short note on HTTP connection pooling and how we account parallel sessions in the rate-limit math (see connection-pool-guidance.txt). Happy to adjust numbers based on your follow-ups.

Rafael Mendes
Enterprise Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
rafael@redwood.com
From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>

Subject: Connection pooling & streaming recommendations

Mike — a few practical details on connection pooling and streaming that affect effective concurrency and rate limits:

- We recommend HTTP/2 with multiplexed streams where possible. A single HTTP/2 connection can carry many concurrent logical streams; however, we also count concurrent active inference requests per stream toward the account concurrent cap.
- For very high concurrent streaming sessions, consider using long-lived connections with periodic keep-alives and a small number of connections per backend host. This reduces TCP overhead and helps with load balancing.
- If your clients create 2–3 streams per user, the effective concurrency per active user is 2–3x; factor that into the pool size.
- For streaming payloads we recommend a smaller per-token commit (to reduce perceived latency) and a larger KV cache budget to avoid recomputation on resumed streams.

Operational knobs for EdgeScale:
- Use client-side circuit-breakers + exponential backoff on 429s; Redwood can add a Retry-After header with suggested backoff windows.
- We can expose a per-route soft quota that returns informative headers (X-Redwood-Quota-Remaining) so your front-end can make informed decisions on connection reuse.

I'll translate your numbers into a first-pass capacity-to-cost estimate and include both hosted and dedicated options in the MAP.

— Marcus
